chunks.text: prolog: hi all, these are largely fragments of what's happening in my life for the past month, some recurrent thoughts, links/reading I like throughout the month of January. This will be the first of many. if you wish not to receive this (though i would love you to have it), well... just let me know.

i. seen.
christmas alone this year. new year too. the logistics matter less than the residue: days stretching without anyone expecting me anywhere, the particular quiet of a city where everyone has somewhere to be that isn’t with you. i cooked pasta for one. watched the steam rise and dissipate. walked queen street in that toronto cold that makes your face feel like a surface, like something that belongs to the weather more than to you.
there was a decision. america was pulling, that gravitational thing, density of interesting people doing interesting things, the spreadsheet pointing south. i talked to N about it. partly because she understands expected value. partly because (and this is the embarrassing part) i wanted permission, a yes from N. i wanted her to say you should go so leaving could feel like following advice rather than what it actually was. she said she wanted me here. selfishly, she added, as if the label would neutralize the desire.
this has happened before: scraped everything at seventeen leaving Vietnam, again at twenty-one for work, again and again, relationships attenuating into messages that grow further apart until they stop. Bridges writes about transitions, how every movement toward something new requires first an ending, then a disorienting middle he calls the neutral zone, then finally a beginning1. i have been good at the endings. less certain i have ever properly arrived at a beginning.
M appeared somewhere in this interval.
we met through a friend actually. then i wrote something public. life-resource-allocation-as-a-problem as I recalled it, which is the title you give distress when you want it to look like philosophy. anyone paying attention could see through it.
M followed. read the thing and sent a message at 19:30 on a tuesday. are you okay?
rosie spinks writes about how friendship has started to feel strikingly similar to admin, scheduled weeks in advance, canceled right before, promising connections that never blossom into quotidian check-ins2. this was the opposite. someone interrupting their own evening to notice i was not okay, without the frictionless machinery of modern social coordination.

M followed. read the thing and sent a message at 19:30 on a tuesday. are you okay?
rosie spinks writes about how friendship has started to feel strikingly similar to admin, scheduled weeks in advance, canceled right before, promising connections that never blossom into quotidian check-ins2. this was the opposite. someone interrupting their own evening to notice i was not okay, without the frictionless machinery of modern social coordination.
sherry ning has this phrase i can’t stop thinking about, sucralose friendships. we have thousands of virtual friends but no one we can ask to feed our cat3. the connections taste sweet but leave no nourishment. i scroll through my phone sometimes and count: how many of these people would i call at 2am? how many would pick up? we mistake the appearance of connection for connection itself, the way you can mistake sucralose for sugar until you notice you’re still hungry.
M’s message wasn’t sucralose.
when my mother asks if i’m okay, the information content is low. she is supposed to ask. the role demands it. but M exists outside the obligation-structure. M could have scrolled past, could have thought that’s heavy and continued with their day. the care means something precisely because nothing required it. esther perel talks about social atrophy, how we’ve eliminated friction from our lives until we no longer know how to deal with people, because people are complex systems4. but M’s message had friction in it. the friction of caring without contract.
i have built an set of persona—the engineer, the student, the host, the wannabe-writter. they are real, and i inhabit them daily, but mostly they function as blocks-for-categorization familiar from the outside looking in. ways of presenting a surface that resembles what everyone does, what society deems acceptable. the reason for their existence is LEGIBILITY. and legibility helps draw the map clearly, helps others locate you within coordinate systems they already understand. in a sense we are all conforming the mud we hide deeply within ourselves into these boxes, pressing the formless into molds, with hopes that the shapes provide solid foundation to go against the currents. yet i fear that if someone tried to excavate the dunes underneath, if someone dug past the neat containers and reached what they were built to conceal, i might not survive such close examination.

M’s attention did not evaluate the surfaces. it passed through them.
Bridges calls the middle stage of any transition the neutral zone, that disorienting place where you’re no longer who you were but not yet who you’re becoming. he says most people don’t understand it, expect to move straight from old to new. but this isn’t a trip across the street. it’s a journey from one identity to another5. i think i have been in a neutral zone for years. maybe since leaving vietnam. the geographic resets are ways of avoiding the psychological passage, substituting external movement for internal transition.
M’s message did something to the neutral zone. cracked it open. made visible the thing i had been avoiding: that underneath all the roles there is a continuous thing that has been waiting to be seen. not evaluated, not assessed. just witnessed.
Dostoevsky’s underground man says he doesn’t want the crystal palace. he wants to want. and i have been like this, outside my own desires, watching them like fish in an aquarium. the sucralose friendships feed this. they give you something to consume rather than inhabit. you become a spectator of connection rather than a participant.
M’s message interrupted the spectatorship. for a moment i was not watching myself be cared for. i was simply being cared for. the recursion collapsed.
I like to quote ava a lot, befriending people who are trustworthy makes you more trusting. secure attachment can be a learned thing. this is the mechanism. M’s care generated something in me. a degree of care that exceeds whatever calculus could justify it. and i find myself wanting to care for others the same way now, freely, gratuitously. the attention multiplied by being received. this is the opposite of sucralose.
i stayed in canada.
i don’t know if it was the right decision. but the spreadsheet doesn’t have a column for someone checked on you and it changed something. maybe it never did. I do like to quote ava quite a bit, again: no one tells us that friendship is a form of redemption because even if work goes wrong and your boyfriend dumps you if you have people who believe you’re going to be okay you believe that you’re going to be okay.
i am still in the neutral zone. something ended that night in december. something is beginning that i don’t have a name for yet.

ii. graduating soon.
i am finishing my degree at McMaster this year. finally. graduation, hmm, where this chapter of my life finally closed. i have been a student for longer than makes sense, stretching what should have been four years into something shapeless, and now the container is closing.
i must confess to being a massive procrastinator. if there is an exam in a week, i will clear every piece of work backlog i’ve been ignoring for months. if there is something urgent due tomorrow, i will write for hours, then pull an all-nighter to make the urgent thing happen anyway. For some reason, whatever is most pressing gets avoided by completing everything else. i believe the degree itself has been subject to this logic. it was always the thing i could defer in favor of whatever felt more alive.
i don’t really like going to school. this sounds ungrateful, i know. education is privilege. i found real satisfaction in philosophy seminars, the particular pleasure of working through a proof or working with professors. but the majority of my time here has been waiting for something to happen that never quite arrived? i came in with a clear vision of what i needed to do, and that vision did not include focusing on schoolwork. so i worked throughout, traded the standard experiences for career progress, told myself this was strategic rather than avoidant.
with that said, a lot of reflection came up as my time at Mac is concluding. you could argue i could have done this reflection anywhere, and you’d be right. but there’s something about the frame dissolving that forces the looking-back:

lossy definition of boundary space.
I would categorize myself as a commuter. Most of my time at Mac were either living off campus to now, living in Toronto. GO train, bus, walk through campus in weather designed to make you question your choices. i spent a lot of time last year at a bar near Locke street, eating pasta, watching people stroll by, asking the chef for recipes they were testing. then i’d walk to an overpriced vegan grocery to buy yogurt that cost 237% more than fortinos.
School gives a lossy structure of what timelines really are. not as tight as sprint deadlines and standup meetings, but enough to anchor a day around assignments, midterms, tests. within that structure, space to experiment with thoughts and idea-space. i spent most of my time working on projects that weren’t school, but i still oriented my days around the academic calendar. being in school gave me an excuse to be lazy, to sit with thoughts without being productive, to let things ruminate and grow organically. permission for drift.
the two-prong approach to freedom.
school doesn’t give you freedom exactly, but it formalizes its absence in a way that creates space. blocks of time structured around deadlines. within those blocks, you can do what you want. it was okay to be in a state of homeostasis. okay to not know yet.
and yet i felt imprisoned by this freeing sense of agency. when you have many things you want to do, what is the point of doing any of them? the clarity of deadlines was scaffolding i could lean against while building something else. now the scaffolding is coming down and i don’t know if what i built can stand alone6.
there’s an imposter quality here. my experience was unconventional in ways that I don’t know what to compare it against. When people were out partying, i was triaging github issues. When people were hanging out with their friends in the library, I was writing reports and finalising design decision for Bento. I built things that weren’t assignments, traded experiences my peers were having for experiences i thought mattered more. I’m fortunate to care about what i do, so the trade didn’t feel like loss. but tiny parts still linger, wondering if a different frost would have made university more enjoyable. if i missed something essential by treating the degree as scaffolding rather than structure.
friends-making-during-university.

friends-making-during-university.
i did not make many friends in university. most came through computer engineering, which is how i met N. there are people you just know will be in your life until the end, and N was one.
Aristotle distinguished friendships of utility (useful to each other), pleasure (enjoyable company), and virtue (mutual admiration for who the other is becoming)7. Growing up in vietnam, most friendships were utility-based. we were all put into this school for gifted kids, and it happened we were in it together. I think this is good for children, as in you create community with people who share similar circumstances to help you grow.
Maybe this is why I didn’t feel a loss of connection with my Vietnamese friends when moving abroad, because I didn’t really have friends from the sense of “i enjoy their character”. I recognized this eventually and cultivated toward a few people (JC, JZ) who still inspire me, to this day. Going into university, i consciously decided not to make friends out of necessity. filters and probes, picking up priors, ensuring connections could survive the impending doom of adulthood. this came with downsides. loneliness, mostly. but i survived, and the friendships that remain feel load-bearing in ways the numerous ones never did.
i think it’s okay to be foreign and not make many friends. we have this notion that you need eighteen people to experience youth together. but if you know what you want, the number reduces to two or five8.

the degree is ending. endings involve disengagement, dismantling, dis-identification. i am disengaging from the student identity, dismantling the structure that gave permission for drift, dis-identifying from the category that explained me to others and to myself. maybe graduation is not about the ceremony or the paper, but a transitory state of being. i have been avoiding this passage by extending the degree, by treating school as an excuse, by dwelling in the in-between as long as possible. the bar on Locke street. the overpriced yogurt. the commute that was part of the escapism from real life.

meaning does not require permanence. this seems important but i am not certain why.

i don’t know what comes after the container closes. most days i operate on habit rather than decision. Camus would continue with full knowledge of the absurd, choosing again each day. i am not certain i achieve this. the degree gave structure to the choosing. without it, the choosing becomes visible, which is uncomfortable, which is maybe the point.
the moment is arriving anyway. i am trying to meet it as something other than deferral.

iii. lost.
we carry fragments of people who have left, and the fragments do not know they are fragments.
i talked with DQM this morning. we hadn’t spoken in a while, and the call was meant to be our monthly updates. but somewhere in the first ten minutes his voice changed, and he told me a friend of his had passed away last month.
he didn’t give details. the facts arrived in pieces, the way they do when someone is still learning how to hold them. an accident. sudden. the kind of thing that happens to other people until it happens to you.
he said everyone seems fine. he said he seems fine. his voice was steady when he said it. but i could see something in his eyes through the screen, a stillness that wasn’t peace. the way someone looks when they’ve decided not to feel something until later, until they’re alone, until it’s safe. i recognized that look. i didn’t say anything about it.
then he said something that seemed to give him comfort. his friend had seen everyone beforehand. the week before, or maybe a few days, there had been a gathering. the people who mattered were there. his friend had been present with the people who loved him, and then he was gone. DQM said this like it was a small mercy, and maybe it was. at least there was that. at least the last memories were warm ones, faces around a table, laughter that no one knew would need to last.
it reminded him of his uncle, he said. the uncle who passed years ago. grief has a way of compounding like that. one loss opens the door and all the others walk back in.
he didn’t say what the hardest part was. but i could infer it from the pauses, from the way his eyes moved when he spoke. the hardest part wasn’t the absence. the hardest part was realizing he had become a different person in that friendship, and now he didn’t know which parts of that person to keep and which to let dissolve. the friend had been a mirror. without the mirror, he couldn’t see clearly enough to know what was his. he didn’t say this. but i heard it anyway.

he didn’t say what the hardest part was. but i could infer it from the pauses, from the way his eyes moved when he spoke. the hardest part wasn’t the absence. the hardest part was realizing he had become a different person in that friendship, and now he didn’t know which parts of that person to keep and which to let dissolve. the friend had been a mirror. without the mirror, he couldn’t see clearly enough to know what was his. he didn’t say this. but i heard it anyway.
i listened. i didn’t know what to say. death is a clean break in one sense, total, unmistakable. you know exactly when it happened. you can point to the date. but the residue doesn’t respect the break. the residue keeps expecting the person to text back.
it reminded me of something. a loss of my own, though different. slower. less legible.
i lost a friend two years ago now. not to death but to the other thing, the drift that happens so gradually you can’t locate the moment it began. we used to talk weekly. then monthly. then the gaps grew longer and neither of us acknowledged them. i would see her name in my phone’s suggestions and feel a small pulse of something, guilt or grief or just the recognition of absence. eventually i stopped feeling the pulse. the name became data, a contact entry with no living referent.
two years. i still don’t know when the friendship ended. that’s the cruelty of drift. death gives you a date, a funeral, a structure for mourning. drift gives you nothing. one day you realize it’s been eight months since you spoke and you can’t remember whose turn it was to reach out, and the not-remembering feels like proof that it doesn’t matter anymore, that whatever you had has already decomposed beyond recognition.
DQM’s loss and mine are not the same. i know this. his friend is gone in a way mine is not. my friend is still alive somewhere, living a life i no longer witness, accumulating experiences i’ll never hear about. and yet there’s something shared in the residue. the phrases you still use. the places you avoid. the way someone can be absent and still distributed across your nervous system like tripwires you forgot you laid.

DQM’s loss and mine are not the same. i know this. his friend is gone in a way mine is not. my friend is still alive somewhere, living a life i no longer witness, accumulating experiences i’ll never hear about. and yet there’s something shared in the residue. the phrases you still use. the places you avoid. the way someone can be absent and still distributed across your nervous system like tripwires you forgot you laid.
i told DQM about the drift. about my friend, two years gone now. about how different it felt from what he was describing but also how the residue seemed to operate by similar laws. he was quiet for a moment. then he said: at least you could have reached out. at least the door was still there, even if neither of you opened it. i can’t reach out. there’s nowhere to reach.
i didn’t have a response. he was right. the door had been there. i hadn’t opened it. two years is long enough that opening it now would feel like archaeology, like disturbing something that has already become historical. the friendship exists only in past tense. but it didn’t have to. that’s the difference. DQM’s friend was taken. my friend and i, we just let it happen. we watched the drift and didn’t swim against it.
[———]
and then there’s the other kind of loss. the one that doesn’t involve another person at all.
i have been losing myself. i don’t know how else to say it. the edges that used to be sharp have blurred. the things i was certain about have become questions. the capacity i once had for feeling, for caring in that unguarded way, has narrowed into something more cautious, more calculated.
i used to be a certain kind of person. i used to love freely, stupidly, without the accounting that comes later. i would cook for people and not keep track of whether they reciprocated. i would give attention without measuring whether i was receiving equivalent attention in return. this felt natural then. it feels impossible now.

i used to be a certain kind of person. i used to love freely, stupidly, without the accounting that comes later. i would cook for people and not keep track of whether they reciprocated. i would give attention without measuring whether i was receiving equivalent attention in return. this felt natural then. it feels impossible now.
somewhere along the way i learned to filter. i learned that humans exploit, that some beings will take whatever care you offer and convert it into resource extraction without ever naming it as such. the learning was necessary. i don’t regret it exactly. but the filtering cost something. the openness narrowed. the default shifted from yes to maybe to prove-it-first. and now i look at myself and i don’t recognize the person who used to dive in without checking the depth.
there’s a towel i kept from when L stayed over. I kept not washing for a while, but then decided to throw it away. keeping it means keeping the rot, letting the memory decay until throwing it away becomes necessity rather than choice. i got a cup of hot chocolate last week and it reminded me of her, and i realized how we carry these fragments without knowing, how someone can be absent and still woven into the substrate of your days. but the towel is also a marker of something else. a version of myself that could still be surprised by intimacy, that hadn’t yet learned to hold everything at arm’s length.
i think about the edges i’ve lost. the sharpness of conviction that used to define me. i knew what i wanted. i knew who i was. i knew what kind of person i was trying to become. now those certainties have softened into something murkier. i still have opinions but they feel less load-bearing. i still have desires but they feel borrowed, like i’m performing wanting rather than actually wanting.
paul shepard wrote that the grief we interpret as a failure in our personality is actually a feeling of emptiness where a beautiful and strange otherness should have been encountered. but what about the emptiness where your own edges should have been? what do you call the grief of losing yourself incrementally, so slowly you can’t point to the moment it happened?

paul shepard wrote that the grief we interpret as a failure in our personality is actually a feeling of emptiness where a beautiful and strange otherness should have been encountered. but what about the emptiness where your own edges should have been? what do you call the grief of losing yourself incrementally, so slowly you can’t point to the moment it happened?
maybe this is just what happens. maybe the edges are supposed to blur as you accumulate experience. maybe the sharpness of youth is just inexperience wearing the costume of certainty. but it doesn’t feel like growth. it feels like erosion. like something is being worn away and i can’t tell if what remains is more essential or just less.
[———]
there’s a line from helena fox: stare into a fire for more than a minute and it’s clear we humans are ridiculous for thinking we’re solid. we are built from nothing, collapsible in an instant. elements arranged, empty atoms ricocheting. we think we’re tangible things, but really we’re just ghosts walking, dust waiting. our insides are made of flickered, fickle light.
maybe the self is just residue. sediment left behind by everyone who has passed through, compacted into something that feels solid but isn’t. maybe loss isn’t losing something you had. maybe loss is discovering that what you thought you had was always borrowed, always on loan from the interactions that constituted it.
DQM’s friend, gone completely but having seen everyone first. my friend, gone differently, two years now. the versions of myself that existed in those relationships, inaccessible. the edges that have blurred. the residue we carry without permission.
i’m still here though. something about the particular arrangement of attention and time. the people who remain. the ones whose fragments i carry and who carry mine.

Jo Malone’s Amber Labdanum Cologne Intense
me and the missus went to do some shopping, and we passed by the Jo Malone shop. amber and labdanum. warm without being cloying. the kind of scent that makes you want to lean closer to a stranger, which is its own kind of danger.
Chloé Zhao Is Yearning to Know How to Love
Zhao talking about loneliness and connection in a way that felt like she was reading from notes i hadn’t written yet. “i’m still learning how to love” from someone who makes films about people learning the same thing.
Language, Truth and Logic by A.J. Ayer + On Certainty by Wittgenstein
reading these back to back creates a strange vertigo. ayer so confident about what can and cannot be said. wittgenstein, later, dismantling the very ground ayer stood on. i keep returning to wittgenstein’s line: “the difficulty is to realize the groundlessness of our believing.”
Who Gets Shipped, and Why?
data visualization about fanfiction pairings. sounds frivolous but it’s actually about how we project desire onto characters, which relationships we find narratively satisfying, what gaps we need fiction to fill. the most shipped pairs are rarely the canonical ones. we want what the text refuses to give us.
Thought as a Technology
michael nielsen on how we’ve figured out ways to display our thoughts onto media that augment cognition. i keep returning to the thurston quote he uses: “how big a gap is there between how you think about mathematics and what you say to others?” the gap is where the interesting stuff lives. the gap is what we’re always trying to close and never quite managing.
The Power of Beauty in Communicating Complex Ideas
beauty as epistemic tool. not decoration but a way of making things legible that wouldn’t otherwise be. i think about this when i cook, when i write, when i try to explain something technical to someone who doesn’t share my vocabulary.
Research as Understanding
kanjun on research as the process of building understanding rather than producing outputs. “the goal is not to produce research artifacts but to change yourself.” this reframes everything. the papers, the code, the essays, they’re byproducts. the real work is the transformation.

remarque


william bridges, transitions: making sense of life’s changes. every transition has three phases: ending (letting go), neutral zone (the disorienting in-between), new beginning. bridges says most people try to skip the neutral zone, to move directly from ending to beginning. this doesn’t work. the neutral zone is where transformation happens. you have to dwell in the confusion. ↩


rosie spinks: friendship has become indistinguishable from admin. plans scheduled around myriad commitments, then canceled. promising friendships never blossom into quotidian check-ins. the crux: we are so burned out by staying afloat in a globalized world that we don’t have energy for the easy interactions that might give us energy back. ↩


sherry ning, stop looking at each other: modern loneliness masks itself as hyperconnectivity. tethered to sucralose friends, torn apart in all directions. we don’t have friends anymore; we have followers. we don’t deeply care about each other’s lives; we consume them as content. ↩


esther perel on social atrophy: we learned social negotiation on the street. we fought, made rules, made peace, developed social muscles. everything about predictive technologies is giving us assisted living. you get it all served without friction, and you no longer know how to deal with people. ↩


bridges: one of the most difficult aspects of the neutral zone is that most people don’t understand it. they expect to move straight from old to new. but this isn’t a trip from one side of the street to the other. it’s a journey from one identity to another. ↩


the freedom paradox: too much freedom collapses into paralysis. we need constraints to generate meaning. school provided artificial constraints that allowed me to build unconstrained things within them. the question is whether the things i built can generate their own constraints now. ↩


aristotle’s three types of friendship from the nicomachean ethics. utility friendships dissolve when usefulness ends. pleasure friendships fade when pleasure does. virtue friendships persist because they’re grounded in character, in mutual admiration for who the other person is becoming. ↩


dunbar’s social brain hypothesis suggests the number of stable relationships a human can maintain is cognitively limited. the innermost circle (about five people) represents those you’d turn to in crisis. where they come from is up to you. ↩
